entities.name: Sauromaces II of Iberia
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sauromaces II, a pivotal figure in the 4th-century geopolitical struggle between the Roman and Sasanian Persian empires, served as King (mepe) of Iberia from 361 to 363 CE and later as a Roman-backed diarch from 370 until his death in 378 CE. A member of the Chosroid Dynasty, his reign was characterized by a protracted contest for control over the strategically vital Kingdom of Iberia (Kartli), situated at the crossroads of East and West. Though largely overlooked by later Georgian historiography, his existence and political machinations are thoroughly documented by the contemporary Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus, whose accounts provide a rare glimpse into the complex dynastic and imperial maneuverings that defined the Late Roman frontier.

His initial ascension in 361 CE saw him briefly displace his cousin, Aspacures II, through Roman intervention, a move quickly reversed by Persian pressure that installed Aspacures III. Sauromaces then spent seven years in exile within the Roman Empire, cultivating alliances until a renewed Roman offensive under Emperor Valens in 370 CE forcibly reinstalled him as a co-ruler alongside Aspacures III's son, Mihrdat III. This diarchy, a Roman attempt to secure influence without outright annexation, effectively split Iberia into Roman and Persian spheres of influence, with Sauromaces governing the western, Roman-aligned territories from his capital at Armazi, while Mihrdat controlled the eastern, Persian-leaning regions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sauromaces II's reign, though brief and contested, significantly impacted the political structure of Iberia by leading to a Roman-imposed diarchy and highlighting the kingdom's role as a battleground between empires. His story illuminates the complex geopolitical dynamics of the 4th-century Caucasus, directly influencing the region's trajectory towards increased external intervention.
